claim: The anterior vermis of the cerebellum is thought to play a key role in transforming vestibular information into an estimate of body motion.
source: The anterior vermis of the cerebellum is thought to play a key role in this transformation, yet how its Purkinje cells transform multiple streams of sensory information into an estimate of body motion remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known concept in the field, though the mechanism is unknown.

claim: Most Purkinje cells dynamically encoded an intermediate representation of self-motion between head and body motion.
source: Most Purkinje cells dynamically encoded an intermediate representation of self-motion between head and body motion.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental recordings.

claim: Purkinje cells responded to both vestibular and neck proprioceptive stimulation with considerable heterogeneity in their response dynamics.
source: Notably, Purkinje cells responded to both vestibular and neck proprioceptive stimulation with considerable heterogeneity in their response dynamics.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The vestibular responses of Purkinje cells were tuned to head-on-body position.
source: Furthermore, their vestibular responses were tuned to head-on-body position.
evidence: This is an experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Neurons in the deep cerebellar nuclei unambiguously encode either head or body motion across conditions.
source: In contrast, targeted neurons in the deep cerebellar nuclei are known to unambiguously encode either head or body motion across conditions.
evidence: This is stated as known information, likely from prior studies.

claim: Combining responses of approximately 40-50 Purkinje cells could explain the responses of deep cerebellar nuclei neurons across all self-motion conditions.
source: Using a simple population model, we established that combining responses of~40-50 Purkinje cells could explain the responses of these deep cerebellar nuclei neurons across all self-motion conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the population modeling analysis performed in the study.

claim: The observed heterogeneity in Purkinje cell response dynamics underlies the cerebellum's capacity to compute the dynamic representation of body motion required for accurate postural control and perceptual stability.
source: We propose that the observed heterogeneity in Purkinje cell response dynamics underlies the cerebellum's capacity to compute the dynamic representation of body motion required to ensure accurate postural control and perceptual stability in our daily lives.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings.

claim: Patients with damage to the anterior vermis of the cerebellum show impaired posture and balance, as well as deficits in motor coordination.
source: Patients with damage to the anterior vermis of the cerebellum show impaired posture and balance, as well as deficits in motor coordination (Diener et al., 1984; Bastian et al., 1998; Ilg et al., 2008; Sullivan et al., 2006; Mitoma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: The anterior vermis has a vital role in the vestibulospinal pathways that generate postural adjustments required to ensure the maintenance of balance during everyday activities.
source: In this context, the anterior vermis has a vital role in the vestibulospinal pathways that generate the postural adjustments required to ensure the maintenance of balance during our everyday activities.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The cerebellum contributes to self-motion perception.
source: Additionally, there is an emerging consensus that the cerebellum contributes to our self-motion perception.
evidence: This is stated as an emerging consensus in the field.

claim: Patients with degeneration of the cerebellar vermis demonstrate reduced perceptual time constants and detection thresholds to externally applied rotations.
source: Indeed, patients with degeneration of the cerebellar vermis demonstrate reduced perceptual time constants and detection thresholds to externally applied rotations (Bronstein et al., 2008; Dahlem et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Vestibular pathways mediating vestibulospinal reflexes and stable perception of self-motion explicitly transform vestibular information from a head-centered to a body-centered reference frame.
source: The prevailing view is that the vestibular pathways mediating vestibulospinal reflexes and the stable perception of self-motion explicitly transform vestibular information from a head-centered to a body-centered reference frame.
evidence: This is stated as the prevailing view in the field.

claim: The vestibular sensory organs are located within the head, making the vestibular system's native reference frame head-centered.
source: The vestibular sensory organs are located within the head, making the vestibular system's native reference frame head-centered (reviewed in Cullen, 2019).
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge supported by a review citation.

claim: Vestibular nerve afferents and their targets in the vestibular nuclei encode information in a head-centered reference frame.
source: In turn, vestibular nerve afferents and their targets in the vestibular nuclei also encode information in a head-centered reference frame (Roy and Cullen, 1998; Roy and Cullen, 2001; Roy and Cullen, 2004; Carriot et al., 2013; Brooks and Cullen, 2014; Sadeghi et al., 2007; Jamali et al., 2009; Cullen and Minor, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: The brain accounts for the position of the head relative to the body for vestibulospinal reflexes to accurately control the musculature required to maintain upright posture and balance.
source: However, the brain accounts for the position of the head relative to the body for vestibulospinal reflexes to accurately control the musculature required to maintain upright posture and balance (Tokita et al., 1989; Tokita et al., 2009 Kennedy and Inglis, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Distinct representations of body versus head motion are encoded by individual neurons in the fastigial nucleus.
source: Indeed, distinct representations of body versus head motion are encoded by individual neurons in the fastigial nucleus (Brooks and Cullen, 2009; Brooks and Cullen, 2014) – the most medial of deep cerebellar nuclei – which lesion studies have shown serves an important role in the control of posture and balance (Thach et al., 1992; Kurzan et al., 1993; Pélisson et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior neuronal recording and lesion studies.

claim: Neck proprioceptors provide the head position information required for the transformation from head-centered to body-centered reference frame.
source: Neck proprioceptors provide the head position information required for this transformation (reviewed in Cullen and Zobeiri, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a review citation.

claim: The integration of neck proprioceptive and vestibular signals is thought to underlie the transformation from a head-centered to a body-centered reference frame in vestibulospinal reflexes pathways and our ability to perceive body motion independently of head motion.
source: Thus, the integration of neck proprioceptive and vestibular signals is thought to underlie the transformation from a head-centered to a body-centered reference frame in vestibulospinal reflexes pathways as well as our ability to perceive body motion independently of head motion (Mergner et al., 1997; Peterka, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: Purkinje cells in the anterior vermis project to the rostral portion of the fastigial nucleus.
source: First, Purkinje cells in this region project to the rostral portion of the fastigial nucleus (Batton et al., 1977; Yamada and Noda, 1987), which lesion studies have shown serves an important role in the control of posture and balance (Thach et al., 1992; Kurzan et al., 1993; Pélisson et al., 1998).
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Inhibition of the cerebellar vermis via continuous theta-burst stimulation impairs the modulation of vestibulospinal pathways that normally accounts for changes in the position of the head relative to the body.
source: Second, inhibition of the cerebellar vermis via continuous theta-burst stimulation impairs the modulation of vestibulospinal pathways that normally accounts for changes in the position of the head relative to the body (Lam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Individual anterior vermis Purkinje cells in decerebrate cats can encode both vestibular and neck proprioceptive-related information.
source: Third, neuronal recordings from anterior vermis Purkinje cells in decerebrate cats have demonstrated that individual neurons can encode both vestibular and neck proprioceptive-related information (Denoth et al., 1979; Manzoni et al., 1998; Manzoni et al., 1999; Manzoni et al., 2004), thereby providing a neural substrate for the coordinate transformation using neck proprioceptive signals to convert head-centered vestibular signals to a body-centered reference frame.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior neuronal recording studies in cats.

claim: Prior studies in decerebrate cats stopped short of establishing whether Purkinje cells integrate vestibular and neck proprioceptive signals to dynamically encode head or body movement.
source: However, these studies stopped short of establishing whether Purkinje cells integrate vestibular and neck proprioceptive signals to dynamically encode head or body movement.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior studies.

claim: Most (~75%) Purkinje cells dynamically encoded an intermediate representation of self-motion between head and body motion.
source: We found considerable heterogeneity across individual Purkinje cells in their encoding of head versus body motion, with most (~75%) neurons dynamically encoding an intermediate representation of self-motion between head and body motion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Bimodal neurons responded to both vestibular and neck proprioceptive stimulation and displayed head-position-dependent tuning in their sensitivity to vestibular stimulation.
source: These neurons, termed bimodal neurons, responded to both vestibular and neck proprioceptive stimulation and displayed head-position-dependent tuning in their sensitivity to vestibular stimulation.
evidence: This is a characterization of bimodal neurons based on experimental data.

claim: A minority of cells, termed unimodal neurons, only responded to vestibular stimulation and unambiguously encoded the motion of the head in space.
source: In contrast, a minority of cells, termed unimodal neurons, only responded to vestibular stimulation and unambiguously encoded the motion of the head in space.
evidence: This is a characterization of unimodal neurons based on experimental data.

claim: The linear combination of a given neuron's response sensitivity to dynamic neck and vestibular stimulation alone well estimated its response during combined stimulation.
source: Across all cells, the linear combination of a given neuron's response sensitivity to dynamic neck and vestibular stimulation alone well estimated its response during combined stimulation.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of neuronal responses.

claim: A simple linear combination model combining the responses of ~40 Purkinje cells could account for the more homogeneous responses of target neurons in the rostral fastigial nucleus during applied self-motion.
source: Finally, we found that a simple linear combination model combining the responses of ~40 Purkinje cells could account for the more homogeneous responses of target neurons in the deep cerebellar nuclei (i.e., the rostral fastigial nucleus [rFN]) during applied self-motion.
evidence: This is a finding from the population modeling analysis.

claim: A sequential transformation from a head-centered to body-centered reference frame occurs between the cerebellum and deep cerebellar nucleus to ensure postural and perceptual stability in everyday life.
source: Our results provide the first evidence, at the level of single Purkinje cells, that a sequential transformation from a head-centered to body-centered reference frame occurs between the cerebellum and deep cerebellar nucleus to ensure postural and perceptual stability in everyday life.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Each Purkinje cell in the population (n = 73) was responsive to vestibular stimulation and was insensitive to eye movements.
source: Each Purkinje cell in our population (n = 73) was responsive to vestibular stimulation and was insensitive to eye movements.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental population.

claim: There was considerable heterogeneity in vestibular sensitivities across the Purkinje cell population.
source: As illustrated in Figure 1A, we found considerable heterogeneity in vestibular sensitivities across our Purkinje cell population.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Some Purkinje cells generated excitatory versus inhibitory responses for oppositely directed head movements (linear).
source: Some neurons generated excitatory versus inhibitory responses for oppositely directed head movements (Figure 1A; left, linear).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Some Purkinje cells generated bidirectional excitatory responses (v-shaped).
source: Alternately, some neurons generated bidirectional excitatory responses (center, v-shaped), while others largely only generated excitatory responses for one movement direction (Figure 1A; right, rectifying).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Vestibular-only neurons in the rostral fastigial nucleus and vestibular nucleus consistently show excitatory versus inhibitory responses for oppositely directed head movements.
source: This contrasts with the vestibular responses recorded in areas targeted by Purkinje cells in the anterior vermis. Notably, vestibular-only neurons in the rFN and vestibular nucleus consistently show excitatory versus inhibitory responses for oppositely directed head movements (rFN: Gardner and Fuchs, 1975; Shaikh et al., 2005; vestibular nucleus: Scudder and Fuchs, 1992; Cullen and McCrea, 1993; McCrea et al., 1999; Roy and Cullen, 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior studies supported by citations.

claim: The preferred movement direction could be either ipsilateral or contralateral for a given Purkinje cell.
source: We found that the preferred movement direction (i.e., the direction that resulted in an excitatory response, or in the greater excitatory response in the case of v-shaped neurons) could be either ipsilateral or contralateral for a given Purkinje cell.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Neurons with preferred responses for ipsilaterally directed rotations were classified as Type I.
source: Neurons with preferred responses for ipsilaterally (n = 32, e.g., Figure 1A, right panel) or contralaterally (n = 41, Figure 1A, left and middle panels) directed rotations were accordingly classified as Type I or Type II, respectively.
evidence: This is a classification scheme used in the study.

claim: 43% of neurons demonstrated responses that were relatively in-phase (±15°) with head velocity.
source: Our analysis further revealed that the response dynamics varied considerably across neurons, with 43% neurons demonstrating responses that were relatively in-phase (±15°) with head velocity (1.8 ± 7.7°), while others demonstrated marked response leads (32%, 57 ± 31) or lags (25%, –47.5 ± 22°).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of neuronal responses.

claim: Most neurons (~75%, n = 54) were sensitive to passive proprioceptive stimulation (bimodal neurons).
source: We quantified the neck proprioceptive sensitivity of each Purkinje cell using least-squares dynamic regression (see Materials and methods) and found that most neurons (~75%, n = 54) were sensitive to passive proprioceptive stimulation (Figure 2B, C, filled bars; bimodal neurons), whereas the remaining ~25% (n = 19) were insensitive (Figure 2, Figure 2B, C, open bars; unimodal neurons).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of neuronal responses shown in Figure 2.

claim: The remaining ~25% (n = 19) of neurons were insensitive to proprioceptive stimulation (unimodal neurons).
source: We quantified the neck proprioceptive sensitivity of each Purkinje cell using least-squares dynamic regression (see Materials and methods) and found that most neurons (~75%, n = 54) were sensitive to passive proprioceptive stimulation (Figure 2B, C, filled bars; bimodal neurons), whereas the remaining ~25% (n = 19) were insensitive (Figure 2, Figure 2B, C, open bars; unimodal neurons).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of neuronal responses shown in Figure 2.

claim: The dynamics of responses to proprioceptive stimulation varied considerably across Purkinje cells.
source: Overall, similar to our findings above regarding vestibular stimulation, the dynamics of responses to proprioceptive stimulation varied considerably across Purkinje cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Purkinje cells showed considerable heterogeneity in their simple spike response dynamics to vestibular versus proprioceptive stimulation.
source: Furthermore, Purkinje cells showed considerable heterogeneity in their simple spike response dynamics to vestibular versus proprioceptive stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neurons typically did not show the same patterns (linear, v-shaped, rectified) to vestibular versus proprioceptive stimulation.
source: Indeed, neurons typically did not show the same patterns (linear, v-shaped, rectified) to vestibular versus proprioceptive stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The vestibular sensitivities of bimodal Purkinje cells were comparable to those of their unimodal counterparts.
source: The vestibular sensitivities of bimodal Purkinje cells were comparable to those of their unimodal counterparts (p = 0.17).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The neck sensitivities of bimodal neurons were most often (67%) antagonistic relative to their vestibular sensitivities in the preferred direction.
source: We further found that the neck sensitivities of bimodal neurons were most often (67%) antagonistic relative to their vestibular sensitivities in the preferred direction.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of neuronal responses.

claim: Relative to vestibular sensitivities in non-preferred direction, bimodal cells were as likely to have antagonistic as agonistic responses to neck proprioceptive stimulation.
source: In contrast, relative to vestibular sensitivities in non-preferred direction, bimodal cells were as likely to have antagonistic as agonistic responses to neck proprioceptive stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unimodal cell response sensitivities were comparable during the vestibular-only and combined stimulation conditions.
source: Consistent with this proposal, we found that unimodal cell response sensitivities (open bars) were comparable during the vestibular-only and combined stimulation conditions (Figure 3D and E, p > 0.22).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Response phases of unimodal neurons were comparable for vestibular-only and combined stimulation conditions.
source: Likewise, response phases of unimodal neurons were comparable for both conditions (preferred: 11 ± 5 versus 11 ± 14; p = 0.21; versus non-preferred: 27 ± 8 versus 14 ± 18; p = 0.77).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The sensitivities of bimodal Purkinje cells were reduced during the combined stimulation condition relative to the vestibular-only condition.
source: Indeed, consistent with this prediction, the sensitivities of bimodal Purkinje cells were reduced during the combined stimulation condition relative to the vestibular-only condition (Figure 3D and E, filled bars, p < 0.027).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The linear summation model provided a good estimate of the gain of the preferred direction responses during combined stimulation.
source: Thus, the summation model provided a good estimate of the gain of the preferred direction responses during combined stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: Estimated and predicted sensitivities and phases were comparable (R2 = 0.77 and 0.75 for sensitivity and phase, respectively, p < 0.001).
source: Overall, estimated and predicted sensitivities and phases were comparable (R2 = 0.77 and 0.75 for sensitivity and phase, respectively, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the modeling analysis.

claim: The slope of the line fitted to the data comparing estimated and predicted values were not different from 1.
source: The similarity between values is shown by the slope of the line fitted to the data which were not different from 1 (p = 0.42 and 0.83 for gain and phase, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the modeling analysis.

claim: Only a minority of neurons were designated as primarily head (26%) or body (2%) encoding.
source: Indeed, only a minority of neurons were designated as primarily head (26%) or body (2%) encoding (light and dark orange bars, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis of neuronal coding properties.

claim: In contrast to Purkinje cells, the majority of rostral fastigial nucleus neurons were designated as primarily head (34%) or body (26%) encoding.
source: In contrast to Purkinje cells, the majority of neurons were designated as primarily head (34%) or body (26%) encoding.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior data from rostral fastigial nucleus neurons.

claim: The vestibular responses of bimodal neurons in the rostral fastigial nucleus modulate as a function of head position.
source: Specifically, the vestibular responses of bimodal neurons in the rFN modulate as a function of head position (Brooks and Cullen, 2009; Kleine et al., 2004; Shaikh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Bimodal Purkinje cells displayed marked changes in vestibular sensitivity with changes in head-on-body position.
source: The example bimodal neuron was typical in that it displayed marked changes in vestibular sensitivity with changes in head-on-body position (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Unimodal neurons did not show evidence for tuning as a function of head-on-body position.
source: In contrast, we did not find evidence for such tuning in unimodal neurons (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Bimodal neurons were more narrowly tuned than were unimodal neurons (mean tuning widths; 7.2 versus 15°, respectively).
source: First, bimodal neurons were more narrowly tuned than were unimodal neurons (mean tuning widths; 7.2 versus 15°, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of experimental data.

claim: There was no difference in the mean of the tuning curve between unimodal neurons and bimodal neurons.
source: Finally, there was no difference in the mean of the tuning curve between unimodal neurons and bimodal neurons (p > 0.37).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The strength of tuning was significantly higher for bimodal rostral fastigial nucleus neurons than Purkinje cells (~30% reduction for Purkinje cells, p < 0.001).
source: Overall, the strength of tuning was significantly higher for bimodal rFN than Purkinje cells (Figure 6D, compare solid gray and black lines, ~30% reduction for Purkinje cells, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Tuning width was reduced for bimodal Purkinje cells (~40% reduction) compared to rostral fastigial nucleus neurons.
source: Tuning width was also reduced for bimodal Purkinje cells (~40% reduction), while mean tuning direction was comparable for both cell groups (p > 0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of experimental data.

claim: Tuning was consistently stronger for bimodal than unimodal neurons in Purkinje cells as has previously been shown for rostral fastigial nucleus neurons.
source: Moreover, tuning was consistently stronger for bimodal than unimodal neurons in Purkinje cells as has previously been shown for rFN neurons (Figure 6D, compare solid and dashed lines).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Single bimodal Purkinje cells generally dynamically encoded intermediate representations of self-motion that were between head and body motion.
source: Instead, single bimodal Purkinje cells generally dynamically encoded intermediate representations of self-motion that were between head and body motion.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Bimodal neurons in the deep cerebellar nuclei dynamically encode body motion.
source: In contrast, bimodal neurons in the deep cerebellar nuclei – the primary target of these Purkinje cells (Figure 7A; rFN) – dynamically encode body motion (i.e., orange shaded region, Figure 5C) and also show stronger vestibular tuning as a function of head-on-body-position.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior data from rostral fastigial nucleus neurons.

claim: The transformation from a head- to body-centered representation of self-motion is achieved by integrating the activities of multiple Purkinje cells.
source: Thus, taken together, our present results suggest that the transformation from a head- to body-centered representation of self-motion is achieved by integrating the activities of multiple Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The weighted activities of ~40 neurons generated responses that well approximated those previously reported for bimodal rostral fastigial nucleus neurons.
source: Importantly, in both cases we found that the weighted activities of ~40 neurons generated responses that well approximated those previously reported for bimodal rFN neurons (Figure 7C, red arrow); the confidence intervals of our model estimations and that of the rFN neural responses completely overlapped for a population of ~40 neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from the population modeling analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A population of 40 Purkinje cells could explain the dynamic representation of body motion across conditions as well as robust encoding of vestibular stimuli as a function of static head position observed in bimodal rostral fastigial nucleus neurons.
source: Thus, a population of 40 Purkinje cells could explain the dynamic representation of body motion across conditions (Figure 7D), as well as robust encoding of vestibular stimuli as a function of static head position observed in bimodal rFN neurons (Figure 7D, right panel).
evidence: This is a finding from the population modeling analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The model weight distributions were similar for linear versus v-shaped versus rectifying Purkinje cells.
source: The model weight distributions were similar for linear versus v-shaped versus rectifying Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the population modeling analysis.

claim: Model weight distributions were similar for bimodal versus unimodal Purkinje cells.
source: Similarly, model weight distributions were similar for (i) bimodal versus unimodal Purkinje cells, (ii) Type I versus Type II Purkinje cells, as well as (iii) Purkinje cells with agonistic versus antagonistic vestibular and proprioceptive responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the population modeling analysis.

claim: The addition of simulated mossy fiber inputs did not dramatically alter the estimate of the Purkinje cell population size required to generate rostral fastigial nucleus neurons responses (~50 versus 40).
source: Overall, we found that the addition of such simulated mossy fiber inputs did not dramatically alter our estimate of the Purkinje cell population size required to generate rFN neurons responses (~50 versus 40; Figure 7—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the population modeling analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: A population of ~40–50 Purkinje cells is required to explain the responses of bimodal and unimodal rostral fastigial nucleus neurons, which matches the value established independently from anatomical studies of Purkinje cell – deep cerebellar nucleus neuron projection ratio.
source: Interestingly, our finding that a population of ~40–50 Purkinje cells is again required to explain the responses of bimodal and unimodal rFN neurons matches the value established independently from anatomical studies of Purkinje cell – deep cerebellar nucleus neuron projection ratio.
evidence: This is a comparison of the modeling results with anatomical data.

claim: The integration of vestibular and neck proprioceptive-related information is required to convert head-centered vestibular signals to the body-centered reference frame required for postural control.
source: The integration of vestibular and neck proprioceptive-related information is required to convert head-centered vestibular signals to the body-centered reference frame required for postural control (reviewed in Cullen, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a review citation.

claim: Most vestibular-sensitive Purkinje cells in the anterior vermis also encode neck proprioceptive-related information.
source: Our recordings in the anterior vermis of alert monkeys demonstrate that most vestibular-sensitive Purkinje cells also encode neck proprioceptive-related information.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Two types of rostral fastigial nucleus neurons have been previously identified in alert monkeys: unimodal and bimodal neurons.
source: Two types of rFN neurons have been previously identified in alert monkeys: unimodal and bimodal neurons (Brooks and Cullen, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Unimodal rostral fastigial nucleus neurons respond to vestibular stimulation during passive rotations and dynamically encode head movement.
source: Unimodal neurons respond to vestibular stimulation during passive rotations and dynamically encode head movement.
evidence: This is a characterization of unimodal rFN neurons from prior studies.

claim: Bimodal rostral fastigial nucleus neurons respond to both vestibular and neck proprioceptive stimulation and dynamically encode body movement.
source: Bimodal rFN neurons respond to both vestibular and neck proprioceptive stimulation and dynamically encode body movement.
evidence: This is a characterization of bimodal rFN neurons from prior studies.

claim: The vestibular and neck proprioceptive sensitivities of bimodal rostral fastigial nucleus neurons are both equal and complementary in sign, so they sum linearly to effectively cancel each other during passive head-on-body rotations.
source: Notably, because the vestibular and neck proprioceptive sensitivities of rFN bimodal neurons are both equal and complementary in sign, they sum linearly to effectively cancel each other during passive head-on-body rotations – a condition in which both sensory systems are activated but the body does not move in space.
evidence: This is a characterization of bimodal rFN neurons from prior studies.

claim: Anterior vermis Purkinje cells were on average more sensitive to vestibular than proprioceptive stimulation.
source: In contrast, here, we found that vestibular-sensitive anterior vermis Purkinje cells were on average more sensitive to vestibular than proprioceptive stimulation and that there was considerable variability in the relative signs of responses to each modality.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: There was considerable variability in the relative signs of Purkinje cell responses to vestibular and proprioceptive stimulation.
source: In contrast, here, we found that vestibular-sensitive anterior vermis Purkinje cells were on average more sensitive to vestibular than proprioceptive stimulation and that there was considerable variability in the relative signs of responses to each modality.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Cancellation of vestibular and proprioceptive inputs during passive head-on-body rotations was the exception rather than the rule for Purkinje cells.
source: As a result, cancellation of these two inputs during passive head-on-body rotations was the exception rather than the rule (i.e., Figure 3B) with the vast majority of bimodal Purkinje cells demonstrating significant modulation in response to passively applied head-on-body rotations.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Unlike bimodal rostral fastigial nucleus neurons, which dynamically encode body motion, bimodal Purkinje cells dynamically encode an intermediate representation of self-motion.
source: Thus, unlike bimodal rFN neurons, which dynamically encode body motion, bimodal Purkinje cells dynamically encode an intermediate representation of self-motion.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Bimodal anterior vermis Purkinje cells displayed vestibular tuning as a function of head-on-body position during horizontal rotations.
source: Notably, bimodal anterior vermis Purkinje cells displayed vestibular tuning as a function of head-on-body position during horizontal rotations.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The tuning of Purkinje cells is similar but not as strong as that shown by downstream bimodal neurons in the target rostral fastigial nucleus.
source: This tuning is similar but not as strong as that shown by downstream bimodal neurons in the target rFN (Brooks and Cullen, 2009), and indeed some rFN neurons do encode vestibular information in a body-centered reference frame for both two-dimensional (Kleine et al., 2004; Shaikh et al., 2004) and three-dimensional (Martin et al., 2018) self-motion.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior data supported by citations.

claim: The modulation of vestibular information by a postural signal becomes more marked in the progression from the cerebellar cortex to the deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: Thus, our present data establish that the modulation of vestibular information by a postural signal becomes more marked in the progression from the cerebellar cortex to the deep cerebellar nuclei.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Nonlinear interactions between neck position and vestibular signals were only in bimodal and not unimodal vestibular Purkinje cells.
source: Interestingly, in the present study, such nonlinear interactions between neck position and vestibular signals were only in bimodal and not unimodal vestibular Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The findings regarding the transformation from a vestibular to head-centered reference frame in the anterior vermis of the alert primate contrast with those of Pompeiano, Manzoni, and colleagues in anesthetized decerebrate cats.
source: Finally, it is noteworthy that our findings regarding the transformation from a vestibular to head-centered reference frame in the anterior vermis of the alert primate contrast with those of Pompeiano, Manzoni, and colleagues in anesthetized decerebrate cats.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior studies.

claim: Pompeiano, Manzoni, and colleagues concluded that the direction of average response vector of Purkinje cells encoding both vestibular and proprioceptive information well corresponded to body tilt – consistent with a complete transformation from head- to body-centered reference frame.
source: Using dynamic tilt stimuli, they concluded that the direction of average response vector of Purkinje cells encoding both vestibular and proprioceptive information well corresponded to body tilt – consistent with a complete transformation from head- to body-centered reference frame (Denoth et al., 1979; Manzoni et al., 1998; Manzoni et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a summary of prior studies supported by citations.

claim: There are significant differences across species regarding how the vestibular system integrates multimodal information even at the first stage of central processing in the vestibular nuclei.
source: Additionally, there are significant differences across species regarding how the vestibular system integrates multimodal information even at the first stage of central processing in the vestibular nuclei (reviewed in Cullen, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a review citation.
